introduction: This foundational level introduces two critical property statutes. The Indian Easements Act, 1882 governs the right to use another person's land (like a right of way or sunlight). The Registration Act, 1908 ensures that property transactions are officially recorded to prevent fraud and establish clear public titles.

core_concepts.title: What is an Easement? (Section 4, Easements Act)
core_concepts.description:
An easement is a right which the owner or occupier of certain land possesses, for the beneficial enjoyment of that land, to do (or prevent something from being done) upon certain other land not his own.
- Dominant Heritage: The land for whose beneficial enjoyment the right exists. The owner is the 'Dominant Owner' (the one who gets the benefit).
- Servient Heritage: The land on which the liability is imposed. The owner is the 'Servient Owner' (the one who suffers the burden).
- Example: A owns a house. To get to the main road, A must walk across B's land. A's land is the dominant heritage, and B's land is the servient heritage.

core_concepts.title: What is a License? (Section 52, Easements Act)
core_concepts.description:
A License is a grant by one person to another of a right to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the grantor, something which would otherwise be unlawful (a trespass).
- Key Feature: A license is purely a **personal right**. It does NOT transfer any interest in the property itself. It cannot be transferred to a third party, and it usually ends when the grantor dies or sells the property. (e.g., Buying a ticket to watch a movie in a cinema hall is a license to enter the hall).

core_concepts.title: Lease vs. License
core_concepts.description:
A highly tested legal distinction:
- Lease (TPA Sec 105): Creates an *interest* in the property. Transfers exclusive possession. Cannot be revoked arbitrarily.
- License (Easements Act Sec 52): Creates NO interest in the property. Does NOT transfer exclusive possession. Can generally be revoked at any time.

core_concepts.title: The Registration Act, 1908: Objective
core_concepts.description: The primary purpose of the Registration Act is the conservation of evidence, assurance of title, and prevention of fraud. It ensures that every person dealing with property can check the public records to see who the real owner is and if there are any pending mortgages or claims on it.

important_entities.name: Compulsory Registration (Section 17, Registration Act)
important_entities.key_fact: Documents that MUST be registered to be valid.
important_entities.significance: Under Section 17, certain documents must legally be registered. The most tested are: (1) Instruments of **Gift of immovable property** (regardless of value), (2) Non-testamentary instruments transferring an interest in immovable property of the value of **Rs. 100 and upwards**, and (3) Leases of immovable property from year to year, or for any term exceeding one year.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Is it mandatory to register a Will (Testamentary instrument) in India? **NO**. Under Section 18 of the Registration Act, the registration of a Will is purely **Optional**. A valid, legally executed unregistered Will carries the exact same weight as a registered Will in the eyes of the law.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Dominant = Demands the right. Servient = Serves the right.
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use this association to instantly recall which landowner holds the right (Dominant) and which bears the burden (Servient).

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever an exam asks 'What is the monetary threshold for compulsory registration of the sale of immovable property under Section 17?', the answer is **Rs. 100 and upwards**.
